questions.stem: A 45 year old teacher has had 5 months of severe exhaustion since a flu-like illness. Marking for an hour leaves her wiped out for two days. She wakes unrefreshed and struggles to follow conversations. She has cut down to two days a week. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Disabling fatigue for over 3 months with post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep and cognitive difficulty, and normal bloods, fits the NICE criteria for ME/CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: cut down to two days a week
steps.x: Fatigue, **post-exertional malaise**, unrefreshing sleep and brain fog for more than 3 months.

elim: Fatigue in depression does not worsen for days after exertion, and there is no low mood.
Widespread pain is the dominant feature.

steps.x: **A. Chronic fatigue syndrome.** NICE ME/CFS: fatigue, PEM, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulty for 3+ months.

questions.stem: A 30 year old man has had 6 weeks of debilitating tiredness after a viral illness. Small amounts of activity make him much worse the next day. He sleeps 10 hours but wakes exhausted and has poor concentration. Examination and baseline blood tests are normal. His pulse rate is 74 bpm.
questions.q: Which additional criterion must be met before chronic fatigue syndrome can be diagnosed?
o: Low mood for at least 2 weeks
Symptoms persisting for at least 3 months
Symptoms persisting for at least 6 months
questions.e: In adults the NICE symptoms must be present for at least 3 months and not be explained by another condition.

steps.x: The question asks: which additional criterion must be met before chronic fatigue syndrome can be diagnosed?

clues: Examination and baseline blood tests are normal
steps.x: The features fit but the **duration** is short.

elim: Low mood is not a criterion and suggests depression.
Six months is the threshold for GAD, not CFS in adults.
That is not a required feature.

steps.x: **C. Symptoms persisting for at least 3 months.** CFS in adults needs 3 months of symptoms.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man has had 7 months of fatigue and low energy. His GP is deciding between chronic fatigue syndrome and depression. He has no suicidal thoughts. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 122/80 mmHg. Baseline blood tests are normal.
questions.q: Which additional feature would most support chronic fatigue syndrome?
o: Feeling better after a brisk walk
Loss of interest in all activities
Low mood most of the day
Symptoms worsen for two days after reading for an hour
questions.e: Post-exertional malaise, after physical, mental or emotional effort, is the hallmark of CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which additional feature would most support chronic fatigue syndrome?

clues: deciding between chronic fatigue syndrome and depression
steps.x: Look for the **hallmark**: worsening after exertion, including mental effort.
**E. Symptoms worsen for two days after reading for an hour.** PEM can follow mental exertion, not just physical.

questions.stem: A 38 year old solicitor has had 8 months of disabling fatigue after a viral infection. Any effort leaves her worse for days and her sleep is unrefreshing. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. Examination and blood tests are normal. She is diagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome.
questions.q: Which additional symptom is she most likely to report?
questions.e: Cognitive difficulty ('brain fog'), poor concentration and word-finding difficulty are common in CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which additional symptom is she most likely to report?
Which option is a CFS symptom and not a red flag?

elim: A red flag, not a CFS feature.
Red flags for infection or malignancy.

steps.x: **A. Difficulty finding words.** CFS brain fog: poor concentration, word-finding difficulty.

questions.stem: A 25 year old woman has had 6 months of disabling fatigue with post-exertional malaise since glandular fever. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg. Examination shows no lymphadenopathy, rash or joint swelling, and blood tests are normal. The GP asks about other symptoms that commonly occur with this condition.
questions.q: Which additional symptom is most consistent with this diagnosis?
o: Recurrent sore throat and tender glands
questions.e: CFS can include sore throat and tender glands, headaches, myalgia and arthralgia without inflammation.

steps.x: The question asks: which additional symptom is most consistent with this diagnosis?

clues: no lymphadenopathy, rash or joint swelling
steps.x: Pick the symptom that fits CFS and is not a sign of another disease.

elim: Inflammatory arthritis; CFS joint pain has no inflammation.

steps.x: **D. Recurrent sore throat and tender glands.** CFS associated symptoms: sore throat, tender glands, headache, myalgia, arthralgia.

questions.stem: A 33 year old man has had 5 months of widespread muscle aches, headaches and exhaustion that is much worse for days after even light gardening. He wakes unrefreshed. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Power is normal. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Myalgia and headaches with post-exertional malaise and normal investigations fit CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: much worse for days after even light gardening
steps.x: Aches plus **post-exertional malaise** with normal tests.

elim: Over 50s, with raised ESR and shoulder girdle stiffness.
Proximal weakness with a raised CK; his power and CK are normal.
He takes no statin, and CK is normal.

steps.x: **A. Chronic fatigue syndrome.** CFS: myalgia and headache with PEM and normal tests.

questions.stem: A 28 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome feels light-headed and has to sit down after standing in a queue for a few minutes. She has no chest pain or blackouts. Her lying BP is 112/72 mmHg. Cardiac examination is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding when she stands for 10 minutes?
o: Fall in BP of 60 mmHg with collapse
Orthostatic symptoms with a rise in heart rate
questions.e: Orthostatic intolerance with dizziness on standing is a feature of CFS and may be found on examination.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding when she stands for 10 minutes?
Dizzy on **standing**: orthostatic intolerance.

elim: Suggests HOCM; heart examination is normal.
Severe orthostatic hypotension is not typical of CFS.

steps.x: **E. Orthostatic symptoms with a rise in heart rate.** CFS: orthostatic intolerance and dizziness.

questions.stem: A 41 year old woman has had 6 months of disabling fatigue after a viral illness. Light housework leaves her bedbound for two days. She feels anxious about her job and says she is fed up, but she still enjoys TV and seeing her sister. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm. Investigations are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: CFS may coexist with anxiety or low mood; the post-viral onset and post-exertional malaise make it the diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
Mood symptoms are present but not dominant; PEM is.

elim: She retains enjoyment; the hallmark here is PEM.
Her worry is about her job; fatigue with PEM dominates.

steps.x: **B. Chronic fatigue syndrome.** CFS often coexists with anxiety or low mood.

questions.stem: A 21 year old student has had chronic fatigue syndrome for 18 months. She has left university, rarely leaves the house and has stopped seeing her friends. She is pacing her activity. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 110/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which complication of chronic fatigue syndrome has she most clearly developed?
o: Loss of education with social isolation
questions.e: Complications of CFS include functional disability, loss of school or work and social isolation.

steps.x: The question asks: which complication of chronic fatigue syndrome has she most clearly developed?
What has she lost?
**B. Loss of education with social isolation.** CFS complications: disability, loss of school or work, isolation, mood, deconditioning.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man has had chronic fatigue syndrome for a year, which began after a flu-like illness. Every few weeks he has a few days of sore throat, aching and feeling feverish, without measured fever. On two such occasions his CRP and white cell count were normal. His pulse rate is 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation for these episodes?
o: Recurrent flu-like symptoms that are part of CFS
questions.e: Flu-like symptoms often mark the start of CFS and can recur intermittently.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely explanation for these episodes?

clues: CRP and white cell count were normal
steps.x: Flu-like episodes with normal markers in known CFS.

elim: No weight loss, cough or night sweats.
CRP and white cells are normal.

steps.x: **C. Recurrent flu-like symptoms that are part of CFS.** CFS flu-like symptoms can recur intermittently.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man has had 8 months of fatigue and post-exertional malaise after a viral illness, with unrefreshing sleep and poor memory. His temperature is 36.7°C, pulse rate 72 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg. Baseline blood tests are normal. He is fully examined.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
questions.e: Examination in CFS is usually normal; abnormal signs point to another diagnosis.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on examination?
Typical CFS with normal bloods.

elim: Suggests heart, liver or kidney disease.
A red flag for lymphoma or infection.

steps.x: **C. No abnormal findings.** CFS: examination usually normal.

questions.stem: A 44 year old IT manager has had 6 months of exhausting tiredness that started after COVID-19. He used to cycle 50 miles a week but a short walk now leaves him in bed the next day. He has gone from full-time work to one morning a week. His pulse rate is 80 bpm. Blood tests are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe fatigue with post-exertional malaise and a major fall in function after a viral illness is CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?

clues: leaves him in bed the next day
steps.x: Post-viral, PEM and a **major loss of function**.

elim: Normal bloods and no GI symptoms.
Deconditioning improves with gradual activity; he crashes the next day.

steps.x: **A. Chronic fatigue syndrome.** CFS: fatigue + PEM + functional impairment.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman has been tired and unfit since a long hospital admission for pneumonia 4 months ago. Her GP is trying to work out whether this is simple deconditioning or chronic fatigue syndrome. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. Blood tests are normal.
questions.q: Which feature would best distinguish chronic fatigue syndrome from deconditioning?
o: Disproportionate worsening of symptoms for days after minor effort
Improvement as activity is gradually increased
Tiredness at the end of a busy day
questions.e: Post-exertional malaise is the hallmark that distinguishes CFS from ordinary fatigue or deconditioning.

steps.x: The question asks: which feature would best distinguish chronic fatigue syndrome from deconditioning?

clues: simple deconditioning or chronic fatigue syndrome
steps.x: What does CFS have that deconditioning does not?
**B. Disproportionate worsening of symptoms for days after minor effort.** PEM separates CFS from deconditioning.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has had 5 months of exhaustion since a viral illness. Walking to the shops leaves her worse for days. She wakes unrefreshed, feels dizzy on standing and cannot concentrate at work. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm lying and 104 bpm standing. Blood tests including thyroid function are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Post-viral fatigue with PEM, unrefreshing sleep, cognitive difficulty and orthostatic intolerance with normal bloods is CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely diagnosis?
PEM plus **orthostatic** symptoms after a virus.

elim: Would cause postural hypotension, pigmentation and abnormal electrolytes.

steps.x: **B. Chronic fatigue syndrome.** Orthostatic intolerance is part of CFS.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man with 7 months of post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep and brain fog after a viral illness has read about 'tests for ME' online. His examination and baseline bloods are normal. His pulse rate is 74 bpm. He asks which test will confirm chronic fatigue syndrome.
questions.q: Which investigation confirms chronic fatigue syndrome?
questions.e: CFS is a clinical diagnosis made after excluding other causes; no confirmatory test exists.

steps.x: The question asks: which investigation confirms chronic fatigue syndrome?
Is there a confirmatory test at all?

elim: Assesses orthostatic intolerance, not CFS itself.

steps.x: **D. No specific test confirms it.** CFS: clinical diagnosis, no confirmatory test.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman presents with 4 months of disabling tiredness that is worse after activity. She has not been seen before for this. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. The GP suspects chronic fatigue syndrome.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step in assessment?
o: Full history and examination to exclude other causes
Tell her it is CFS and begin pacing
questions.e: First-line is clinical assessment to exclude other causes of chronic fatigue.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate first step in assessment?

clues: not been seen before for this
steps.x: A **new** presentation of fatigue.

elim: NICE advises against graded exercise therapy; and assessment comes first.
Other causes must be excluded first.

steps.x: **B. Full history and examination to exclude other causes.** Exclude other causes before labelling CFS.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman has 4 months of fatigue, worse after exertion, and unrefreshing sleep. She has very heavy periods. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. A full blood count shows haemoglobin 118 g/L (115–165) with a borderline low MCV.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional blood test?
questions.e: Ferritin is part of the CFS baseline panel to exclude iron deficiency, a common mimic in a woman with menorrhagia.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate additional blood test?
Menorrhagia and a low-normal MCV: **iron**.
**C. Serum ferritin.** CFS baseline includes ferritin, B12 and folate.

questions.stem: A 46 year old woman has had 5 months of tiredness. She has also gained 5 kg, feels cold and is constipated. Her pulse rate is 58 bpm and BP 126/82 mmHg. Her skin is dry. She asks if she has chronic fatigue syndrome like her friend.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Baseline bloods in suspected CFS include TFTs to exclude hypothyroidism, which these features suggest.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
Classic **hypothyroid** features.
**D. Thyroid function tests.** Exclude hypothyroidism before diagnosing CFS.

questions.stem: A 39 year old man has had 4 months of fatigue, worse after effort. He also has early morning stiffness in his hands lasting an hour and occasional low-grade fevers. His temperature is 37.6°C, pulse rate 88 bpm and BP 128/80 mmHg. Thyroid function and full blood count are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: CRP and ESR in the baseline panel help exclude inflammatory disease, which morning stiffness and fevers suggest.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Inflammatory clues: check **inflammatory markers**.
**B. CRP and ESR.** Baseline CFS bloods include CRP/ESR to exclude inflammation.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman has 6 months of fatigue, worse after exertion, with poor concentration. She has been vegan for 4 years without supplements and has tingling in her feet. Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. Thyroid function and ferritin are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: B12 and folate are part of the baseline panel; an unsupplemented vegan diet with paraesthesia makes B12 deficiency likely.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next investigation?
Diet without B12 and neuropathy.
**E. Serum B12 and folate.** CFS baseline: FBC, U&E, LFT, TFT, CRP/ESR, glucose, B12, folate, ferritin.

questions.stem: A 37 year old woman has had chronic fatigue syndrome for a year. Her baseline blood tests were normal. She has been mostly at home resting. Her temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 84 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg. Her GP examines her at review.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Tired appearance with non-specific muscle tenderness
Wasting of the small muscles of the hand
questions.e: Examination in CFS is usually normal but may show a tired appearance, non-specific tenderness, orthostatic symptoms or deconditioning.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely finding on examination?

clues: chronic fatigue syndrome for a year
steps.x: Which option is benign and consistent with CFS?

elim: Suggests motor neurone disease or cord pathology.

steps.x: **D. Tired appearance with non-specific muscle tenderness.** CFS exam: normal, or tired, tender, deconditioned.

questions.stem: A 33 year old woman has had 6 months of fatigue with post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep and brain fog. Baseline tests are normal. She has seen three doctors and says she feels nobody believes her. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate first step in management?
o: Confirm and validate the diagnosis with her
questions.e: The first step is to confirm and validate the diagnosis with the patient.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate first step in management?
She needs the diagnosis **acknowledged**.

elim: NICE advises against graded exercise therapy for ME/CFS.
For sleep or pain, not the first step.
CFS is not a psychiatric diagnosis.
They are normal; repeating delays care.

steps.x: **A. Confirm and validate the diagnosis with her.** Step one in CFS: confirm and validate the diagnosis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old man with newly diagnosed chronic fatigue syndrome has been told by friends to 'get fit' by going to the gym every day and pushing through. His pulse rate is 72 bpm. Last week a gym session left him bedbound for three days.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Balance activity and rest to stay within his energy limits
questions.e: Energy management (pacing) balances activity and rest to stay within limits and avoid relapse.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate advice?
Overexertion causes a crash.

elim: Graded exercise therapy is not recommended.

steps.x: **A. Balance activity and rest to stay within his energy limits.** Pacing: activity within energy limits, not pushing through.

questions.stem: A 39 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome is pacing well. She is offered cognitive behavioural therapy and is upset, saying it means her doctor thinks the illness is 'all in her head' and that therapy will cure it. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate explanation of the role of CBT?
o: It cures CFS in most patients
It is only for patients with depression
It supports symptom management as part of a package and is not a cure
It treats the cause of the illness
questions.e: CBT supports symptom management and assists rehabilitation; it is not a cure but part of a supportive package.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate explanation of the role of CBT?
Two misunderstandings: cause and cure.

elim: It is offered to support management in CFS.
The cause is unclear; CBT is supportive.

steps.x: **D. It supports symptom management as part of a package and is not a cure.** CBT in CFS: supportive, not curative.

questions.stem: A 34 year old man with chronic fatigue syndrome is pacing his activities. He now has frequent throbbing headaches with nausea and light sensitivity lasting several hours. Neurological examination is normal. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 118/76 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management of his headaches?
o: No treatment as they are part of CFS
Treat the headaches directly according to their type
questions.e: Associated problems in CFS, such as headache, sleep disturbance and pain, are managed directly.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate management of his headaches?

clues: throbbing headaches with nausea and light sensitivity
steps.x: A treatable symptom alongside CFS.

elim: No red flags; neurological examination is normal.

steps.x: **D. Treat the headaches directly according to their type.** Treat CFS symptoms such as headache directly.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome finds it very hard to get to sleep. She naps for 3 hours each afternoon, uses her phone in bed until 2am and drinks coffee in the evening. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 114/70 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management of her sleep problem?
questions.e: Sleep disturbance in CFS is managed directly, starting with sleep hygiene.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate initial management of her sleep problem?

clues: uses her phone in bed until 2am
steps.x: Clear behavioural causes of poor sleep.

elim: Hypnotics cause dependence; long courses are avoided.

steps.x: **D. Sleep hygiene advice.** CFS sleep problems: treat directly, starting with sleep hygiene.

questions.stem: A 42 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome is pacing, but poor sleep and widespread aching are limiting her. She is sensitive to medicines. Her GP decides to start amitriptyline. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg. ECG is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate way to start amitriptyline?
o: 10 mg at night, increased slowly with monitoring
150 mg at night from the start
questions.e: Low-dose tricyclics are started low and increased gradually and individually, monitoring for side effects, to improve sleep and pain.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate way to start amitriptyline?
Low dose, at night, go slow.

elim: Not the dosing pattern; it is given at night.
Too high and sedating by day.

steps.x: **A. 10 mg at night, increased slowly with monitoring.** Amitriptyline in CFS: low dose, gradual, monitored.

questions.stem: A 37 year old nurse with chronic fatigue syndrome wants to stay in work. Twelve-hour shifts leave her bedbound for days, but she manages well on shorter shifts. She is pacing and her sleep has improved. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next step to support her function?
o: Graded exercise to build stamina for long shifts
Occupational health referral for workplace adjustments
questions.e: Supporting function includes occupational support and work adjustments.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate next step to support her function?
She can work with **changes** to her job.
**D. Occupational health referral for workplace adjustments.** CFS: occupational, school and work adjustments.

questions.stem: A 44 year old man has had chronic fatigue syndrome for 2 years. He is pacing, taking low-dose amitriptyline and has adjusted hours at work. His symptoms are stable. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. He asks what follow-up he needs.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term plan?
o: Stop all treatment as he is stable
questions.e: Long-term management of CFS includes regular follow-up review.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most appropriate long-term plan?
Stable but chronic.
**D. Regular follow-up review.** CFS: regular review long-term.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with severe chronic fatigue syndrome lives alone. A friend reports he has lost 8 kg in a month, is too exhausted to prepare food or wash and has barely drunk for 2 days. His pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg. His mucous membranes are dry.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Profound functional decline, dehydration or malnutrition, or inability to self-care needs urgent or emergency review.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the next most appropriate step in management?

clues: too exhausted to prepare food or wash
steps.x: Dehydrated, malnourished and cannot self-care.

elim: Not recommended and he is unwell.

steps.x: **E. Urgent same-day medical assessment.** CFS red flags: dehydration, malnutrition, cannot self-care.

questions.stem: A 35 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome asks what causes her illness. She has post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep and orthostatic dizziness. Her blood tests have all been normal. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm.
questions.q: Which best describes the current understanding of the pathophysiology?
o: Demyelination of the central nervous system
Immune dysregulation with abnormal central and autonomic nervous system responses
questions.e: CFS is a complex multisystem condition of unclear aetiology, thought to involve immune dysregulation and abnormal central and autonomic responses.

steps.x: The question asks: which best describes the current understanding of the pathophysiology?
Multisystem, unclear cause.

elim: It is a multisystem condition, not purely psychiatric.
Infection is a trigger, not ongoing active infection.

steps.x: **E. Immune dysregulation with abnormal central and autonomic nervous system responses.** CFS: immune, autonomic and energy metabolism dysfunction.

questions.stem: A researcher studies muscle from patients with chronic fatigue syndrome. They have disabling fatigue and post-exertional malaise. Their routine blood tests are normal. She is investigating the cellular process thought to explain why energy runs out so quickly.
questions.q: Which cellular process is most likely to be under study?
o: Acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction
questions.e: Mitochondrial and energy metabolism dysfunction is one proposed mechanism in CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which cellular process is most likely to be under study?

clues: why energy runs out so quickly
steps.x: Energy production in the cell.
**D. Mitochondrial energy metabolism.** CFS: mitochondrial/energy metabolism dysfunction.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome had a good day and walked into town. She felt fine at the time, but the next day she could not get out of bed and remained much worse for four days. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm.
questions.q: Which best explains this pattern?
o: An abnormal, disproportionate response to exertion
Low mood after a stressful day
questions.e: Post-exertional malaise is an abnormal, disproportionate worsening of symptoms after even minor exertion, distinguishing CFS from deconditioning.

steps.x: The question asks: which best explains this pattern?

clues: remained much worse for four days
steps.x: Delayed and **disproportionate** crash.

elim: No trauma and no localised pain.
Would be immediate, not delayed for days.
Deconditioning causes tiredness at the time, not a delayed crash.

steps.x: **B. An abnormal, disproportionate response to exertion.** PEM: delayed, disproportionate worsening after exertion.

questions.stem: After a large outbreak of a viral infection in a boarding school, several pupils develop disabling fatigue with post-exertional malaise lasting over 3 months. Their viral tests are now negative and routine bloods are normal. The school doctor asks why the illness followed the infection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: An aberrant or persistent immune response triggered by the infection
questions.e: CFS frequently follows infection, suggesting an aberrant or persistent immune or inflammatory response in some cases.

steps.x: The question asks: which is the most likely explanation?

clues: why the illness followed the infection
steps.x: The virus has gone, but the response has not.

elim: Bloods are normal and the trigger was viral.

steps.x: **A. An aberrant or persistent immune response triggered by the infection.** Post-viral CFS: aberrant persistent immune response.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man with chronic fatigue syndrome sleeps 10 hours a night but always wakes exhausted. He has no snoring or witnessed apnoeas. He also becomes dizzy when standing. His pulse rate is 72 bpm lying and 102 bpm standing.
questions.q: Which mechanism is thought to contribute to both his unrefreshing sleep and dizziness?
questions.e: Autonomic dysfunction is thought to contribute to both orthostatic intolerance and unrefreshing sleep in CFS.

steps.x: The question asks: which mechanism is thought to contribute to both his unrefreshing sleep and dizziness?
One mechanism linking sleep and posture.

elim: Not suggested and not the CFS mechanism.

steps.x: **A. Autonomic dysfunction.** Autonomic dysfunction: unrefreshing sleep and orthostatic intolerance.

questions.stem: A 32 year old woman has had chronic fatigue syndrome for 3 years and has spent most of it in bed. Her fatigue is now worse than at the start, and she becomes breathless walking to the bathroom. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm. Repeat bloods are normal.
questions.q: Which best explains the progressive worsening of her fatigue?
o: Inactivity causing deconditioning that perpetuates fatigue
questions.e: Prolonged disability leads to secondary deconditioning, which perpetuates fatigue and lowers exercise tolerance in a self-reinforcing cycle.

steps.x: The question asks: which best explains the progressive worsening of her fatigue?
Years of inactivity.
**B. Inactivity causing deconditioning that perpetuates fatigue.** Disability -> deconditioning -> more fatigue: a vicious cycle.
